newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK lawmakers seek to avert Chinese crackdown.
newsitem.headline: HK lawmakers seek to avert Chinese crackdown.

text.p: In a last stand against a possible Chinese crackdown, Hong Kong's lame-duck legislature on Tuesday passed laws minimising punishment for political dissent after British rule ends.

As Governor Chris Patten presided over the last cabinet meeting of British colonial rule east of Suez, before Hong Kong returns to China next week, pro-democracy legislators scraped together sufficient votes to strike down proposed provisions against subversion and secession.

The outgoing colonial government had tabled bills against subversive activities. But pro-democracy lawmakers feared China might use the laws to suppress freedom of speech and other political activities.

By 23 votes to 20, the elected Legislative Council -- which will die alongside British rule at midnight next Monday -- amended laws so that they state clearly that only violence, and not vocal dissent, will amount to a punishable offence.
The legislators also made clear that seditious statements in speeches or publications will not be against the law.
China had strongly criticised earlier drafts of the law, accusing Britain of meddling in the affairs of the post-colonial government, but had stopped short of saying it would scrap the measure.
Hong Kong's stock market maintained its ebullient demeanour on Tuesday amid the final flurries of 150 years of British rule.
It retained enough confidence to ride out Wall Street's biggest fall for seven years, losing just one percent on the day.
The commander of the fast-dwindling number of British forces in Hong Kong embraced the mood of optimism.
He even gave a ringing vote of confidence to Chinese forces that will replace his troops, describing them as "warm and intelligent people".
Major-General Bryan Dutton said Chinese troops scheduled to enter Hong Kong hours before its handover posed no threat.

"The Royal Hong Kong Police are in control both before midnight and after midnight," he said. "The (Chinese) military presence here is purely as a manifestation of sovereignty, a largely ceremonial role.
"As individuals they are warm and intelligent people. Ultimately they are cautious still because they are children of their system just as I am a child of our system."
On Monday Britain agreed that 509 of China's People's Liberation Army (PLA) troops could cross the border at 9pm on June 30 in order to be in position in Hong Kong at midnight.
There were no tears and few signs of regret when Patten presided over Hong Kong's inner "cabinet" for the last time.

Midway through what was described as a very businesslike meeting, Patten's Executive Council -- comprising three top civil servants and eight appointed high-flying members from Hong Kong'e elite circles -- took a break to pose for the media.
"All of us today, we look at a city which is one of the greatest cities in the world," Patten said with pride at the results of his five years in charge of Britain's last major colony.

Most of Patten's advisers will not serve beyond the handover when a team headed by Beijing's chosen leader, Tung Chee-hwa, will take over and set the broad directions for government of the territory of 6.4 million.
Patten's popular deputy Anson Chan, Chief Secretary and head of the civil service, will transfer to Tung's Executive Council, along with outspoken Financial Secretary Donald Tsang.
